items.content:
AI won’t fix a messy process.

It will read the mess faster.

If the standard lives in someone’s head, AI has no stable context.

If every shift does the work differently, AI sees variation.

If handoffs happen by memory, AI misses the real constraint.

Before you automate anything, map the current state.

One process.
One whiteboard.
One real flow.
One painful bottleneck.

Stabilize first and automate second...

The floor tells the truth.

items.content:
Most waste does not look dramatic.

This picture shows the 8 wastes neatly. On the floor, they don't show up like icons on a poster. They show up as habits.

A defect that gets reworked without a word.
A part that arrives late, every cycle.
A cart pushed farther than it needs to, every shift.
A box of WIP that has been sitting in the corner for weeks.
An operator who knows the fix, and nobody asks.

This is what waste actually looks like.

It looks like a NORMAL Tuesday.

At the machine.
At the weld bench.
At the assembly station.
At the loading dock.

Small moments, repeated thousands of times, baked so deep into the day that nobody sees them anymore. The supervisor walks past the same waiting operator every morning and counts it as normal.

Waste is not the dramatic event. It is the routine you stopped questioning.

Lean's real work is making the routine visible again. Walk the floor without a clipboard. Watch one operator. Count the moments where nothing is moving forward. Then ask why.

That is where the 8 wastes actually live.

The floor tells the truth. Every workaround is a system failure. Stability first. Everything else follows.

This is operations.

The question for leaders is simple:

Do your people feel safe enough to tell you what is really happening?

items.content:
A standard is only useful while it still matches the floor.

The problem starts quietly.

The process changes.
The best operator finds a better way.
The shift adapts.
Nobody updates the standard.

Then the standard becomes decoration.

The binder says one thing.
The CNC operator does another.
The night shift does a third.

New people learn from whoever is nearby.
Experienced people work around the process. Supervisors chase the same mistakes every week.

A standard your best operator ignores is not a standard.

If the most experienced person on the floor works around the process, the process is the problem.

The workaround becomes the real method.

It lives in one head.
It works.
Until that person leaves.

That’s where AI earns its place on the floor.

Small, focused tools that keep work instructions alive.

Updated from real performance.
Updated from real problems.
Updated by the people doing the work.

The standard becomes a living document.

Same standard.
Every operator.
Every shift.

Start with one question:

Which process depends most on one person knowing how?

That’s the first standard to fix.

Because without standard work, AI only makes chaos faster.

Stability first. Everything else follows.

Where does tribal knowledge hurt your operation the most?

items.content:
Kaizen, Lean, and Six Sigma are often put in the same bucket.
But they are not the same thing.

Kaizen is the daily habit of improvement.
 Small changes. Operator involvement. Better work every day.

Lean is the operating system.
 Remove waste. Improve flow. Create value with less chaos.

Six Sigma is the precision tool.
 Reduce variation. Use data. Attack defects with discipline.

The mistake is choosing one like it is a religion.

The better question is:

What problem are we solving?

If the floor is chaotic, start with Lean.
 If people are disengaged, start with Kaizen.
 If defects are repeating, bring in Six Sigma thinking.

Tools do not fix factories.

People using the right tool for the right problem do.

items.content:
My sensei Gary said something years ago that I still come back to.

“Accepting Lean is like changing religion. And how often do people actually change religion?”

That line explains more about failed Lean transformations than most maturity models I’ve seen.

You can teach someone 5S in an afternoon.

Standard work.
Value stream mapping.
Kaizen events.
Visual boards.

The mechanics are simple.

The belief underneath is the hard part.

That problems are normal and worth surfacing.

That the person closest to the work knows something the org chart doesn’t.

That stopping the line to fix a defect is strength.

That daily improvement matters more than the perfect rollout plan.

That’s a worldview.

And worldviews don’t change because someone ran a workshop.

I’ve watched plants put up the boards, run the huddles, hang the templates, and change almost nothing.

The methodology was borrowed.

It never became how the operation actually worked.

So what moves people across that line?

Proof.

Someone tries one small change.
It holds.
Their day gets easier.
The problem comes back less often.

Then the belief starts to move.

One person at a time.

Slower than any rollout plan wants. But much stronger when it sticks.

Most transformations install the tools and wait for belief to follow.

I think it works the other way around.

The proof comes first.
Then belief follows...

items.content:
If air freight is a regular habit, it’s usually not a freight problem.


(It’s a planning inputs problem.)


Two small process fixes took a client from weekly air shipments to quarterly.


Here’s how it happened:
1) Cleaned up and improved their demand signals

2) Rebuilt their safety stock calculation to actually reflect lead time and demand variability

More accurate supply plans meant fewer emergency gaps and fewer gaps meant fewer “we need this now” air shipments.

The solve wasn’t a new system or a big investment.

Which exactly why I like starting with small, high-leverage process fixes: they reduce firefighting with a realistic level of effort.

Solid planning inputs, revisited consistently, can realistic have large impacts.

If your ERP is “the source of truth,” why does everyone still live in Excel?


I used to think it was only a legacy-system problem.

But I’ve seen it in plenty of modern environments too—across industries and company sizes.

Here’s the pattern I keep running into:

Spreadsheets don’t show up because teams love spreadsheets. They show up because teams are trying to solve one of three gaps:

Trust gap (the ERP data is wrong or inconsistent)

Fit gap (the ERP can’t flex to how the business actually runs)

Visibility gap (people can’t validate what’s behind the number)


And once a spreadsheet becomes the “real” planning file, it quietly changes how decisions get made.

items.content:
The old playbook: One central fulfillment node. Simple, clean, easy to manage.

The new playbook: Expand into multiple nodes. Get closer to your customer. 

The smarter playbook: It actually depends — and getting it wrong is expensive either way. 


Here's what I've seen play out recently with two CPG brands in the health and wellness space: 

Brand A came to me operating out of two fulfillment locations. On paper it made sense. 

In practice? 

They were a wholesale-driven business with a leaner team, and the complexity was quietly killing them. Inventory split across two nodes meant they couldn't optimize levels at either one — which led to chronic stockouts that were frustrating their retail partners. 

The fix was consolidating to one central node. 

Simpler inventory management, lower carrying costs, fewer headaches for a team that didn't have the bandwidth to manage the complexity. 


Brand B was the opposite story. A DTC-first business shipping from one central location — with over 30% of their orders traveling to zones 6-8. 

They had the team, the right logistics partners, and the volume to justify a second node. 

The projected savings? $250K annually just in outbound shipping costs. 

Same industry. Completely different answers.

 I believe the brands that win in the next era of fulfillment won't default to "one node" or "many nodes" — they'll ask better questions first. 

What does my channel mix look like? Where does my customer actually live? What can my team and partners realistically support? 


Network design is a lever for better performance and cost savings and knowing when to pull it in either direction leads to better outcomes in the long run.

items.content:
You can have the “right” planning software and still have bad planning.


Because the real question is: is your planning process built for the stage you’re actually in?


This is the framework I use to help clients make that call — from early-stage founders all the way to brands doing mass wholesale.

Planning complexity (in real life) tends to evolve like this:

1) Early-stage (single channel, lean SKU count) → Demand is easier to read. Supply is more direct. Fewer moving parts.

2) Growing multichannel (DTC + wholesale, expanding SKUs) → Demand signals multiply. Fulfillment gets more complex. Forecasting becomes a cross-functional sport.

3) Mass wholesale (broad network, high SKU count) → Supply networks layer. SKU velocity behaves wildly differently across the catalog. Retailer behavior starts driving the forecast (POs, chargebacks, replenishment cycles).


The constants — regardless of stage:
-Your model is only as good as the data you trust

-Planning is only as good as the alignment conversations around it

-Cadence beats sophistication (re-forecasting + scenario planning)


When a client works through this framework, they can immediately spot where they’re overbuilt (wasting time) or underbuilt (risking bigger problems later).

And if you’re waiting for “enterprise tools” before you plan well — you can stop waiting. 

Get the basics right, keep them consistent, and scale them as complexity shows up.

We were watching inventory drop day by day.


(And a supplier shortage meant it could turn into a sales problem fast.)

One thing I wish I knew earlier in my career about contingency planning:

The relationships you maintain when you don’t need them are the ones that save you when you do.

Earlier this year, a primary supplier hit an unexpected materials shortage and we were running dangerously low on inventory—the kind of low where you’re doing the math daily and hoping your timeline holds.

The thing that saved us was a former co-manufacturer we’d worked with for two years before switching to another provider.

We hadn’t given them a PO in a while—but we stayed in touch, kept the relationship warm, and treated them well on the way out.


One phone call later, they moved quickly to source materials and get our production scheduled.

We got inventory out the door in time.

If that relationship had gone cold, we would’ve been starting from scratch in the middle of a crisis—vetting someone new while the clock was ticking.

Your contingency plan is only as strong as the relationships behind it.

Secondary suppliers, backup co-mans, alternative logistics providers—they’re not just names on a list. 

They’re relationships that need attention even when everything is running smoothly.

My dad had a boat that rarely worked properly.



Every summer, my siblings and I spent long days helping him sand, refinish, and paint it. We came home sunburnt, covered in varnish, and exhausted. 

It wasn’t glamorous. But there was something deeply satisfying about taking something worn down and leaving it better than you found it.


That principle has followed me into every engagement I’ve taken on.


Earlier in my consulting journey, I stepped into a client situation where a lot was on fire: process breakdowns, an overcomplicated supply structure, teams working in silos with little visibility into what anyone else was doing—and morale that reflected all of it.


I could have focused purely on operational fixes. But I had this clear feeling that the process problems and the people problems were connected.


So alongside the operational improvements, we built in regular cross-functional touchpoints, created collaborative project plans with clear accountability, and made space for teams to actually communicate with each other. Slowly, trust started to build.


And then you could feel the shift: teams that had been siloed started to see operations not as a source of friction, but as a function that was there to help them.


That moment when the energy in a room changes is one of the most rewarding parts of this work.

items.content:
Operationally, the ultimate goal of selling across multiple channels isn't just more revenue — it's building one flexible pool of inventory that can support all of them.

When inventory is siloed, you end up stocked out on DTC while pallets of the same SKU sit allocated to wholesale. Meanwhile, a retail order comes in and no one has visibility into what's actually available to promise.

That flexibility needs to extend to how and where orders get fulfilled too. 

Can you shift volume between fulfillment nodes? 

Can you fulfill a wholesale order from a 3PL that typically handles DTC? 

Have you thought through contingencies if one channel spikes unexpectedly?

This is what it actually means to operate as a true multichannel business — not just selling in multiple places, but building a supply chain nimble enough to support it.

The goal isn't perfection, sales spikes happen and production delays occur. The goal is keep sales flowing with a productive inventory pool with minimal disruptions.

items.content:
Preparing for a major product launch? Easy.

Just do these 5 simple steps:

Line up your co-manufacturer months in advance ✅

Nail down every component of your BOM ✅

Execute a flawless tech transfer from your old co-man to your new one ✅

Watch a key component get stuck in your new co-man’s supply chain and threaten your entire launch timeline ✅

Panic.

Simple! See you at launch day! 🎉

Okay, jokes aside.

We were mid-tech transfer—moving to a turnkey model with a new co-manufacturer—when they hit trouble sourcing a critical component in time for our launch window. 

The clock was ticking, and my first thought was, “Are we really about to delay this over one part?”

The obvious options were to scramble for a new supplier or push the launch.
Instead, we paused and took stock of what we actually had. 

Sitting at our old co-manufacturer? The exact raw material needed.

We sold the component directly to the new co-man, kept the timeline intact, and launched without a hitch.

No new budget. No new vendors. No drama.

The lesson I took from that moment: when things go sideways, your first instinct doesn’t have to be spending more or adding more. Sometimes the solution is already somewhere in your supply chain and you just have to go find it.


Resourcefulness will always beat budget.

items.content:
I was tasked with modeling how much warehouse space a client would need during peak season.

On paper, it sounds straightforward.

In reality, the pressure is that if your inputs are messy, your “answer” looks confident… and still leads you straight into a capacity problem.

So I started with the unglamorous part:

1️⃣ I made sure all logistics specs for their SKUs were documented and up to date. Simple, but everything downstream depends on it.

2️⃣ I built a more detailed inventory model with a week-over-week view, so we could see where inventory swelled and dipped throughout the month.

3️⃣ We aligned on the “rules” for ordering by category (because different categories created very different outcomes).

4️⃣ Then I pulled it all into one model that summed weekly pallet-position needs by storage area against current warehouse capacity constraints.


The result: transparency on what storage needs to prioritize, plus a clear map of which weeks were close to (or over) capacity so we could build a solid gameplan for the next several months.

If you’re heading into peak, what’s the one piece that feels hardest to get clean right now: the data, the rules, or the model?

The delay email hit—and my stomach dropped.


Earlier this year, I was managing a PO for a co-manufacturer that needed to feed directly into a display build for a client, timed to help their team get ahead of their busy season.

Then the timeline started slipping. Once… then again… then again. Weeks of delays.

Sitting in our warehouse was returns inventory that hadn’t been touched. We QC-ed it, re-packed it, and repurposed it for the display.

The client’s team stayed on track for their busy season. No drama. No scramble.

That moment reminded me: operations rewards steadiness. 

When you stay calm, you see the puzzle—not just the pressure.

items.content:
Bad metrics make demand planners look bad.

This infographic shows the 7 critical metrics for demand planners to track:

# 1 - Forecast Accuracy (at the right level)
↳ How close the forecast is to actual demand at the level where decisions are made (SKU-family, product family, region)
↳ WMAPE = Σ |Actual − Forecast| / Σ Actual

# 2 - Forecast Bias
↳ Whether the forecast is systematically over- or under-stated over time
↳ Bias = Σ (Actual − Forecast) / Σ Forecast

# 3 - Forecast Value Add (FVA)
↳ Whether the demand planning process improves or degrades the forecast compared to a baseline 
↳ FVA = Accuracy_after − Accuracy_before; Positive FVA → planning added value; Negative FVA → planning added noise

# 4 - Demand Volatility (Coefficient of Variation)
↳ How unstable demand is relative to its average
↳ Coefficient of Variation (CoV) = Standard Deviation of Demand / Mean Demand; Higher CoV = more volatile, less predictable demand

# 5 - Consensus Forecast Accuracy
↳ How accurate the final, cross-functional forecast is after Sales, Marketing, and Finance inputs
↳ Consensus Accuracy = |Actual − Consensus Forecast| / Actual
 
# 6 - Forecast Timeliness / Stability
↳ How much the forecast changes after it should be locked
↳ Forecast Stability = |Forecast_t − Forecast_t−1| / Forecast_t−1
Or % Changed Volume = Volume changed after freeze / Total forecast volume

# 7 - Forecast Accuracy vs Inventory Outcome
↳ Whether forecast accuracy actually translates into better inventory and service results
↳ Excess Inventory ≈ Over-forecast × Unit Cost; Stockouts ≈ Under-forecast × Demand Shortfall 

Any others to add?

items.content:
A demand planner is NOT a supply planner.

This infographic compares both roles:

Focus
↳ Demand planner: prediction of the future demand
↳ Supply planner: optimization to accomplish demand plan

Key activities
↳ Demand planner: identify anomalies in data and refine forecasts
↳ Supply planner: plan capacity and inventory to align with demand

Stakeholders
↳ Demand planner: CEO, marketing, sales, new product introductions, finance, supply planning
↳ Supply planner: manufacturing/operations/production, materials, procurement, finance, demand planning

Negotiation skills
↳ Demand planner: to navigate internal politics and communicate gaps against the plan
↳ Supply planner: to secure favorable terms with demand planners, production managers and suppliers

Data
↳ Demand planner: uses models to predict demand; POS data, shipments, orders
↳ Supply planner: uses models to optimize capacity, resources, inventory 

Demand
↳ Demand planner: unconstrained demand
↳ Supply planner: turns unconstrained demand into constrained demand

Metrics
↳ Demand planner: FVA (forecast value added), MAPE, WMAPE, bias
↳ Supply planner: OTIF (on time in full), fill rate, lost sales, inventory turnover

Technology
↳ Demand planner: advanced forecasting and data representation tools
↳ Supply planner: ERP, planning systems and inventory management tools

Impact on financials
↳ Demand planner: revenue (top line)
↳ Supply planner: cost (bottom line)
Note: late shipments or shortages can also impact the top line

Any others to add?

items.content:
S&OP is NOT about the past.

You can't change the past.
If you can't change it, it's NOT S&OP.

Many companies spend most of their S&OP meetings reviewing last month's numbers.

Hours discussing:
↳ Last month's actuals vs. forecast
↳ Last month's OTIF
↳ Last month's inventory levels
↳ Last month's production performance
↳ Last month's misses
↳ Last month's explanations

Of course, you need to understand what happened.

But only for one reason:
To make better decisions about the future.

S&OP is not a KPI review meeting.
Finance closes the books.
S&OP changes the future.

Every discussion in an S&OP meeting should end with a decision about the future:
↳ Should we approve overtime?
↳ Should we delay a promotion?
↳ Should we secure additional supplier capacity?
↳ Should we commit to unconfirmed customer demand?

If a discussion doesn't influence a future decision...

It belongs somewhere else.

Not in S&OP.

The past explains.

S&OP decides what happens next.
